author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Sea Glass Orchard
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
Tamsin had drawn the orchard in blue pencil because she thought the blue made the argument more convincing.

She unfolded the plan across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with four stones. Outside, the tide was retreating, leaving dark streaks on the repaired dock. Maui was carving something into the end of a broom handle. He said it was a decorative fish. It looked like a fish trying to escape a terrible situation.

"An orchard?" I asked.

"A sheltered growing space," Tamsin corrected. "Don't tell people I've promised trees."

There were six raised beds on her sketch, two narrow paths, a low wall of reclaimed stone, and a series of open channels leading away from the beach. The paths curved around the old signal post rather than through it.

"Why the channels?"

"Saltwater doesn't care how pretty your lavender is. If a wave comes over the barrier, I want it to leave again."

Maui examined the drawing.

"I could build you a wall high enough to stop any wave."

"Then you'd stop the wind," Tamsin said. "And the rain would collect behind it. And the marsh birds would lose their landing."

"Ah."

"That's one problem with high walls. They solve the thing you can see."

I traced a finger around the empty beds.

"We could invite everyone to plant something."

Tamsin gave me a long look.

"Everyone?"

"People have gardens in their homeworlds. We could make this a place to share cuttings."

"Would you put a mountain fern next to a saltmarsh reed?"

"I'd ask somebody who knows plants."

"Good. I'm somebody."

She turned the sketch over. On the back was a list of species and soil conditions: sea kale, beach peas, saltgrass, two varieties of hardy lavender, and a climbing vine from the sheltered slopes. Alongside each name she'd written where its roots belonged, what water it tolerated, and how far it might spread.

I noticed three names crossed out.

"Why not these?"

"Because one drinks too much freshwater, one strangles everything it climbs, and one is beautiful for a season before its roots crack the stone."

I thought of the way people talked about Lanternweald as though its doors meant they could bring any piece of home through and set it wherever they wished.

"Then we need a steward," I said.

"We have one."

She pointed out the window.

Fen was kneeling beside the brackish pool, checking the tide mark with a ruler. They had been maintaining the coastal channels long before anybody thought to make them fashionable.

"Have you asked Fen what they want?" Tamsin said.

I had not.

Maui, who had been listening very carefully while pretending not to, put down his unfinished fish.

"I could ask."

Tamsin smiled without mercy.

"One of you should."

We went to the shore.

Fen listened to the orchard idea with the expression of someone hearing that a beloved relative wanted to keep six goats in the sitting room.

"People want to plant," I explained.

"People always want to plant. Nobody wants to pull up dead stems in February."

"We'll make a rota."

"Who checks the water salinity? Who notices when the drainage channel silts over? Who tells a visitor their favorite plant can't survive here?"

I looked at the sand beneath my boots.

"That last one might have to be me."

Fen raised an eyebrow.

"You were going to invite everyone."

"I was going to invite everyone to contribute," I said, feeling the distinction form as I spoke. "Not invite everyone to do whatever they please."

"Better."

They led us around the old signal post. The ground dipped into a sheltered crescent, protected from the strongest wind by a ridge of stone. Tiny white flowers grew between patches of saltgrass.

"This is a nursery already," Fen said. "The plants are small because they've been fighting to stay here. Dig all of them up and you'll spend two years trying to replace what you didn't notice."

Maui crouched beside the flowers.

"They're brave."

"They're plants," Fen replied.

"Brave plants."

I smiled.

Fen wasn't smiling.

"They keep the sand from moving. That's their job. The orchard needs to work with them."

We walked the ground, marked where water actually flowed, and drew a revised plan. The best place for the raised beds was smaller than Tamsin's sketch. The old nursery would remain untouched. Paths needed to be wide enough for a handcart and for people who couldn't step down over the rocks. We would use soil already available from a failed market planter rather than hauling peat from another world.

The work didn't look as impressive.

It looked possible.

By afternoon, three more people had arrived to offer their opinions. Mara wanted edible herbs for the kitchen. Iroh had a small cutting of rosemary that needed more sun than his terrace offered. Pip wanted a bed of flowers for the Lantern Walk. Edda wanted a resting bench where the path bent toward the shore.

I wrote every suggestion down.

Maui looked over my shoulder.

"You're making a book of wishes."

"Then tomorrow we compare it to the book of water."

"Less romantic."

"Much more useful."

We held the first gathering by the signal post at dusk. Fen explained which species were suited to the salt spray. Tamsin showed the revised layout. When someone proposed a little grove of fruit trees, another resident explained the roots would reach the drainage stones. Nobody shouted. Somebody looked disappointed. That was allowed.

Mara brought a basket of bread, which helped.

The group agreed to trial three raised beds first. One would hold edible coastal plants, one would be a small nursery for hardy flowers, and one would test the dry-slope herbs. Everything would be labeled with the plant's water needs and origin, not just its pretty name. A spring review would decide whether to add more.

After the meeting, I remained behind to pick up the sketches.

Maui stood beside the old signal post, looking at the dark water.

"You wanted something bigger," he said.

"I did."

"Disappointed?"

"A little."

He considered that.

"That's odd. I thought you loved gardens."

"I do."

"Then why does a smaller one make you sad?"

I looked at the three little rectangles marked on the sand.

"Because I wanted everyone to feel welcome. I imagined that meant saying yes to every idea."

He leaned against the post.

"People used to say yes to everything I promised. I thought they liked me."

"And?"

"They liked the promise. Then I had to become big enough to keep it."

I folded the sketches.

"You're getting annoyingly wise."

"I've had excellent instruction."

"Don't tell me where."

He grinned and took my hand.

The wind had grown cool. It smelled of wet stone and the distant bakery chimney. Maui rubbed his thumb over my knuckles and waited until I looked at him.

"Can I offer one thing that doesn't have to fit the plan?" he asked.

"What?"

"A bench. Just one. Where somebody can sit without feeling obliged to talk."

I pictured Edda's proposed resting place.

"That absolutely fits the plan."

"Then I'm a genius."

"Let's not get carried away."

He kissed my forehead, then the corner of my mouth. The warmth of him against the evening air made it difficult to remember the precise dimensions of a raised bed.

"Come home," I said.

"Gladly."

The next morning, Fen showed us where to set the first stones. Maui carried them without making a speech. I planted a sprig of saltgrass at the edge of the new path and found the ground colder than I expected.

By the time the sun was up, we had one bed, two drainage channels, and no promise of a perfect orchard.

It was the most honest garden I'd ever helped begin.
